Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong
never allow myself to feel or express anger
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you

vignette: Jay, a 27-year-old South Eastern Asian male and journalist, has experienced significant distress following a traumatic event involving physical abuse by his romantic partner. This experience has profoundly altered how he perceives himself and the world around him. Jay's trauma-related events often trigger intense emotional reactions, especially when he is on public transport like buses or when he finds himself alone with men. Jay's self-blame rumination has become a dominant coping mechanism, as he dwells incessantly on what he might have done wrong to provoke such abuse. This constant self-criticism exacerbates his feelings of inadequacy and fuels his tendency to suppress anger. He often restricts his food intake as another way to cope with the emotional turmoil. The triggers not only lead to these maladaptive strategies but also intensify his intrusive memories, making it difficult for him to function normally. The memory of the traumatic event feels present rather than past, causing Jay immense pain and emotional overwhelm whenever it resurfaces. This overwhelming recollection is deeply linked to his fear that such harm could happen again, reinforcing his mistrust in others and his own inadequacy. He believes he can never truly know who might harm him and therefore finds himself constantly vigilant. Jay's fears about potential harm are heightened by his negative appraisals, which create a sense of perpetual threat. When something takes longer than expected or when he wakes during the night to check if he is safe, these moments reinforce his belief that he cannot trust safety even when others assure him it exists. His internal narrative further deepens this mistrust and fear. His negative appraisals also influence his triggers, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of distress. When Jay encounters situations similar to those during the traumatic event, such as being alone with men or riding the bus, he becomes hyper-aware and experiences intense emotional reactions. The feeling that he cannot trust others and is inadequate makes him more susceptible to these triggers. In his role as a journalist, Jay often finds himself in public spaces where encountering potential triggers is inevitable. He has begun to avoid certain assignments that require travel by bus or interactions with male colleagues alone, which has impacted both his professional life and personal relationships. His partner notices the changes but struggles to understand why he withdraws so frequently. Jay's constant state of alertness and avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on his well-being and daily functioning. He finally decided to seek help after a particularly distressing incident where he had a panic attack while alone with a male colleague at work. This experience was the tipping point, as it made him realize that his fears were escalating and affecting his ability to maintain professional relationships. Jay is most afraid of never truly feeling safe or being able to trust others again. He hopes for support in understanding why these memories continue to feel so present and how he can manage his overwhelming emotional reactions without resorting to maladaptive coping strategies. Despite the ongoing struggle, Jay remains hopeful that with help, he can reclaim a sense of control over his life.
